About

Muneeb HassanTopi, PK

Muneeb studied metallurgy the way most people study a language they intend to live in — deliberately, from the crystal lattice up. At PIEAS he graduated with a 3.50/4.0 GPA on a full merit scholarship, and spent his final year chasing a question that still occupies him: could a high entropy alloy be engineered to absorb and release hydrogen at room temperature, without the energy penalty that keeps most metal hydrides impractical? The resulting thesis won PIEAS's Best Final Year Project award.

That question turned into a career. He now works as a Materials Engineer at GIKI, where he runs the vacuum arc melters, ball mills, and characterization equipment that turn alloy compositions into data — and where his current project applies the same high-entropy design logic to water-splitting electrocatalysts, looking for cheaper alternatives to noble-metal catalysts like RuO₂.

Alongside the hydrogen work, he's published on a chemical method for removing support structures from 3D-printed titanium parts, synthesized 2D MXenes and graphene from first principles, and picked up hands-on welding and inspection training along the way. The throughline is consistent: materials problems that sit between the lab bench and the energy grid.

Research

Six problems, one material family at a time.

Each area below sits inside a shared question — how do you design a material's composition to unlock a property nature didn't give it by default.

MgH₂ · HEA

Hydrogen Storage

Award-winning thesis work engineering high entropy alloy compositions that absorb and release hydrogen at room temperature, cutting the energy penalty that limits conventional metal hydrides. Funded by the National Center for Nanotechnology, PIEAS.

Reduced MgH₂ activation energy by 15%, improving kinetics and cycling stability while achieving room-temperature absorption/desorption.

HEA · OER

Water Splitting

An ongoing project at GIKI, designing high entropy alloy electrocatalysts for alkaline water splitting — a lower-cost route to clean hydrogen than noble-metal catalysts.

HEA compositions synthesized by vacuum arc melting and ball milling show markedly lower OER overpotential than benchmark RuO₂. Leading a 4-member GIKI–PIEAS team.

The compositional design thread running through both the storage and catalysis work — multi-principal-element alloys engineered for properties no single-metal system provides on its own.

01 — Thesis Project

High Entropy Alloy Hydrogen Storage

A room-temperature route to storing hydrogen in metal, engineered through a five-plus-element alloy composition rather than a single metal hydride. Funded by the National Center for Nanotechnology, PIEAS.

Problem

Conventional hydrides like MgH₂ store hydrogen densely but need high temperatures to release it — impractical for real-world systems.

Approach

Designed HEA compositions via vacuum arc melting and ball milling to lower the activation energy barrier for hydrogen release.

Characterization

XRD, SEM, TGA, and TPD to track phase composition, morphology, and desorption behavior.

Outcome

Room-temperature hydrogen absorption/desorption with improved cycling stability, delivered two weeks ahead of schedule.

15%
Lower MgH₂ activation energy
4

Schematic illustration In Progress · GIKI, 2025–

02 — Ongoing Project

HEA Electrocatalysts for Water Splitting

The same high-entropy design logic, aimed at a different reaction — a search for a cheaper alternative to noble-metal catalysts in clean hydrogen production.

Problem

Efficient water electrolysis depends on scarce, expensive catalysts like RuO₂ and IrO₂, limiting hydrogen production at scale.

Approach

Synthesized HEA electrocatalysts by vacuum arc melting and ball milling, exploiting compositional complexity for catalytic activity.

Characterization

Cyclic voltammetry, EIS, and LSV to evaluate OER overpotential and electrochemical stability.

Outcome

The optimized HEA electrocatalyst reached a markedly lower overpotential than benchmark RuO₂ — a step toward noble-metal-free electrolysis.

03 — Published Research

Chemical Support-Structure Removal for 3D-Printed Titanium

A commercially viable chemical alternative to mechanical post-processing of complex 3D-printed Ti6Al4V parts, developed with the Pakistan Institute of Additive Manufacturing.

Problem

Mechanical removal of support structures wastes material and risks damaging intricate 3D-printed geometries.

Approach

Developed and tested 12+ chemical etching formulations, optimizing for commercial scalability and surface integrity.

Characterization

SEM to verify surface integrity; cost-benefit analysis to quantify commercial viability.

Outcome

A cost-effective, low-waste process ready for production integration, published in a peer-reviewed journal.

35%
Less material waste
40%

Publications

Peer-reviewed, and in progress.

One published paper so far, with the water-splitting electrocatalysis work moving toward a manuscript.

Rapid Prototyping Journal · December 2025

A simple chemical method to remove the support structure of 3D printed Ti6Al4V alloy

Muneeb Hassan, Aqeel A. Khurram, Numan Ghazali

This paper presents a chemical etching route for removing support structures from 3D-printed Ti6Al4V parts as an alternative to mechanical post-processing. Across more than a dozen formulations, the optimized process reduced material waste by 35% and processing time by 40% relative to mechanical removal, while a cost-benefit analysis showed a 50% reduction in overall cost — with surface integrity confirmed by SEM.
